findings.title: Halt-clear / resume transition undecided — standby-flap write-availability oscillation unbounded
findings.detail: Reasoning frame: 'what breaks if this is wrong?' — §3 decides the primary halts create-path writes on synchronous-standby loss (fail-closed, RPO=0 preserved), which closes the prior P1 CHAOS-ADR-01-001. But the decision names only the entry into the halted state, never the exit. It is undecided whether create-path writes auto-resume when the standby reconnects or require operator action, and there is no guard against standby flapping (standby bouncing up/down) driving repeated halt/resume churn — a write-availability oscillation that, under legitimate load with client retries, can present as a retry-storm against the shorten path each time writes briefly re-open. §7 instruments standby loss (alert <=30s) but no signal or time bound governs recovery detection or a debounced resume. The failure lifecycle is half-specified: clean fail-closed entry, undefined recovery.
findings.recommendation: Decide the resume semantics in §3: auto-resume on confirmed standby re-sync vs operator-gated resume, and if auto, add a debounce / hysteresis bound (e.g. require N seconds of healthy replica-lag-0 before re-opening writes) so a flapping standby cannot oscillate the create path. Add a §7 'standby recovered / writes resumed' signal with a time bound to mirror the existing <=30s loss alert.

findings.title: Create-path halt duration is unbounded — sustained single-standby outage is a distinct availability mode not related to RTO
findings.detail: The fail-closed create-path halt can persist for the entire duration the synchronous standby is down. RTO <= 30 min (§2) is defined for store loss via standby promotion — a different failure than a sustained single-standby outage where the primary survives but shorten stays halted. Detection of standby loss is bounded (<=30s, §7), but the create-path OUTAGE ENVELOPE on that branch has no stated bound and no relationship drawn to the 99.9% availability target or the 30-min RTO. A reader cannot tell how long shorten may be down before recovery escalation (e.g. promote-and-reseed) is expected, so the worst-case shorten-availability blast on the halt branch is unspecified.
findings.recommendation: State the recovery escalation for a sustained standby outage (how long the create-path halt is tolerated before an action — re-provision standby, or promote/reseed — is triggered) and relate it to the availability budget. Even a one-line 'halt tolerated up to T, then escalate to <action>' closes the C3 gap on the halt branch.

findings.title: Planned standby maintenance trips the create-path halt — routine ops becomes a shorten outage (MVP single standby)
findings.detail: The MVP topology is exactly one primary + one synchronous standby (§3 line 126). Because §3 halts create-path writes whenever the synchronous standby is unavailable, any PLANNED standby operation — patching, restart, version upgrade — trips the same fail-closed halt as an unplanned loss, taking the shorten path down during routine maintenance. This is a concrete accidental-failure scenario (a benign operator restarting the standby to patch it causes a create-path outage) that the ADR does not acknowledge. With a single standby there is no maintenance path that keeps writes available.
findings.recommendation: Acknowledge in §7 that planned standby maintenance trips the create-path halt under the MVP single-standby topology, and state the operational handling (maintenance window with shorten degraded-mode advertised, or note that the 'Next cycle' read-replica/standby fan-out provides a maintenance-without-halt path). This makes the accepted ops cost explicit rather than a surprise.
